children: Businesses are increasingly integrating sustainability with supply-chain risk, cost management and operational resilience as disruptions reshape corporate priorities

The need to balance sustainability commitments with cost pressures and supply-chain resilience emerged as a key theme at the 9th Sustainable World Conclave 2026, where industry leaders discussed how companies can maintain environmental goals amid inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and operational disruptions.

Tarika Kumar, Deputy Executive Director, Climate Action and Sustainability, CII-ITC Centre of Excellence for Sustainable Development, said the sustainability debate has moved beyond simply establishing its importance, with businesses now facing the challenge of balancing environmental commitments against operational and economic pressures.

“The debate is no longer whether sustainability matters, but how businesses navigate commitments amid inflation, geopolitical tensions, supply-chain disruptions and rising cost pressures,” Kumar said.

The panel, titled “Sustainability Vs Supply Chain Resilience: What Happens When Cost Comes First?”, featured Thakur Pherwani, Chief Sustainability Officer, TVS Motor; Shilpashree Muniswamappa, Director – ESG & Communications, Colgate-Palmolive India; and Chitra Byregowda, SVP and Global Head of Sustainability & ESG, Persistent Systems. The session was chaired by Kumar.

Pherwani said sustainability should be viewed through the lens of business continuity rather than as a separate corporate objective. “Sustainability is all about de-risking the business,” he said, pointing to the relationship between supplier disruptions and production continuity. “If our supplier gets disrupted, my entire production will get disrupted. And if that gets disrupted, entire business continuity will get disrupted.”

He said TVS Motor had focused on strengthening its value chain following disruptions after the pandemic, with the company reporting that 97 per cent of its value chain was within a 500-km radius of its operating locations during its 2021-24 period.

The company subsequently began mapping Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers through its in-house “My Sustainability Index”, while also working with critical suppliers on energy, production and operational capabilities during periods of disruption.

Pherwani said organisations should not treat sustainability measures as optional during crises. “No matter what crisis it is, great organizations never take a step back in terms of doing away or trade-off in terms of that we will not be working on some of those measures which are going to enhance our sustainability journey or excellence over a period of time.”
He also pointed to sustainable finance, supplier capability building, resource efficiency and workforce support as mechanisms that can strengthen smaller suppliers while reducing business risk.

For Colgate-Palmolive, Muniswamappa said sustainability has to coexist with affordability and consumer expectations. “Customers and consumers may not necessarily buy your product just because of the fact that you're sustainable or just because of the fact that you're organic,” she said. “There must be a very small fraction of it. Especially for consumer goods like ours, you are supposed to be affordable.”

She said consumers increasingly examine labels, ingredients and company claims, making transparency important for brands. The company has also worked on packaging changes, including removing aluminium from toothpaste tubes and increasing the use of recyclable materials.

At Persistent Systems, Byregowda said sustainability decisions increasingly need to be connected to financial and operational data. She highlighted challenges in collecting reliable ESG information from smaller suppliers, particularly across non-IT procurement. “Will your carbon management tool or any other risk management tool be able to provide this data as a single source of information? Today, it's no,” she said.

Byregowda said embedding sustainability within business-unit budgets and using mechanisms such as internal carbon pricing can help companies connect environmental impacts with financial decisions. She also highlighted the shift towards more detailed Scope 3 emissions calculations instead of relying solely on spend-based estimates.

The discussion also touched on extended producer responsibility, waste traceability, recycling infrastructure and the difficulties smaller suppliers face in building ESG capabilities. The panel concluded that supply-chain resilience and sustainability are increasingly interconnected, with companies being pushed to address environmental performance alongside cost, risk and business continuity.
